title: Cosy Nook
strapline: A soft, enclosed little den where a child can retreat, rest and simply be — a right to withdraw, honoured.
intent: Children get a legitimate place to withdraw from a busy room without leaving it — a safe base to return to.
Children who tire or overload easily can rest and recharge before rejoining, rather than tipping into meltdown.
Children learn that needing time alone or quiet is normal and allowed, not naughty or antisocial.
Children experience the deep comfort of an enclosed, softly lit space — a felt sense of safety.
Children begin to recognise their own need for downtime and take themselves off to meet it.
implementation: Create genuine enclosure — a draped canopy, a pop-up tent, a corner behind low shelving — so it feels held and separate, but stays within adult sightlines.
Make it soft and low-arousal: cushions, a rug, a sheepskin, dimmable or fairy lighting, muted colours, no clutter or noisy toys.
Keep it screen-free and calm — a few well-loved books, a soft toy, a family photo — a place to be, not a place to be entertained.
Protect it as a retreat, never a punishment: no child is ever sent there, and time-out has no place here.
Model using it yourself for a quiet cuddle and a book with a child who's had enough, so it reads as care.
Keep numbers low — one or two children — and gently support turn-taking so it stays genuinely calm.
key_questions: Would you like some quiet time in the cosy nook?
How does your body feel in here — softer?
Shall I read with you, or would you rather be on your own for a bit?
Are you ready to come back and play, or do you need a little longer?
What makes this a nice place to rest?

impact.text: Children use a trusted space as a safe base to withdraw to and return from.
Children begin to regulate big feelings using strategies that work for them, with adults nearby not in charge.
Children know their own feelings have names and have at least one thing that helps them calm.
Children begin to know what their body needs — rest, calm, quiet — and do something about it.
Children choose favourite books and handle them, reading to themselves or a soft toy.

enhancements: A basket of calming sensory items — a lava-lamp-style bottle, a soft weighted toy, a texture cushion.
A gentle 'nook is busy / nook is free' sign children learn to read, protecting the calm.
Family photos laminated on the wall of the den for a child who's missing home.
A low-light version for the baby room — a canopied corner for winding down before sleep.
A basket of feelings books to browse quietly when big emotions need naming.

playing_exploring: Children explore the comfort of enclosure and soft textures at their own pace.
The nook invites gentle, self-directed pottering — a book, a cuddle, a look at the lights.
active_learning: Children learn to take themselves off to recharge, then re-engage — a lasting self-care habit.
Returning to play calmer and readier rewards the choice to rest.
creating_thinking: Children begin to read their own body and feelings and decide they need a break.
They work out what helps them settle here and seek it out again.
